module: Neonatal Cholestasis, Metabolic Liver Disease and Cirrhosis

steps.say: Jaundice past two weeks of age is never just breast milk jaundice until you prove it. Split the bilirubin: a direct fraction above one milligram per decilitre, or above a fifth of the total when the total is high, means cholestasis until disproven. That single fraction redirects the baby from reassurance to urgent workup. The hour based nomogram here reminds you that all jaundice starts with timed assessment before fractionation decides the path.
steps.tx: Apply the **biochemical definition of cholestasis** to every prolonged jaundice. Direct or conjugated bilirubin above 1.0 mg/dL (17 mcmol/L) regardless of total bilirubin (or direct above 20% of total if total bilirubin exceeds 5.0 mg/dL) mandates urgent workup for biliary or hepatocellular disease. Fractionate bilirubin in any jaundice persisting beyond 14 days, in any pale stool or dark urine, and before attributing jaundice to breast milk. Cholestasis is never physiological, so a raised direct fraction always triggers the full diagnostic cascade.

steps.say: Parents see nappies every day, so teach them to read the stool like a test strip. Pale clay stools with dark yellow urine flag blocked bile flow weeks before the baby looks ill. Stool colour card screening catches those acholic stools early and pushes biliary atresia evaluation before thirty to forty five days, when surgery still saves the liver. The atretic duct and Kasai loop drawing shows exactly the anatomy that early operation restores.
steps.tx: Run **acholic stool card screening** for every newborn with prolonged jaundice. Infant stool color card screening programs identify persistent pale acholic stools (clay coloured, bile absent) to prompt evaluation for biliary atresia before 30-45 days of age. Counsel that pale stools plus dark urine plus persistent jaundice equals emergency referral, and demonstrate normal versus abnormal colours with the card itself. Kasai portoenterostomy (the Roux loop drainage operation drawn here) succeeds best when performed within this early window.

steps.say: Alagille syndrome hides in plain sight because its clues scatter across organs. A jaundiced infant with a triangular face, a heart murmur and butterfly vertebrae carries one diagnosis until proven otherwise. The inheritance is dominant, so one affected parent often shows only a murmur or eye finding. Behind it all sits a faulty Notch signal, with JAG1 carrying the blame in the vast majority and NOTCH2 in a sliver.
steps.tx: Test **Alagille syndrome genetics** in syndromic cholestasis. Alagille syndrome is an autosomal dominant multi-organ disorder caused by mutations in JAG1 (94-96% of cases) or NOTCH2 (1-2%), encoding Notch signaling ligands (cell fate messengers for bile duct formation). Examine parents for subtle features, since variable expression leaves many carriers mildly affected. A positive gene result explains the liver disease plus cardiac, vertebral, eye and facial findings as one syndrome rather than coincidental anomalies.

steps.say: Liver biopsy still earns its place when genes and scans equivocate. Count bile ducts against portal tracts: fewer than four ducts per ten tracts marks true paucity, far below the normal nine to eighteen. That single ratio separates Alagille duct loss from the ductular riot of biliary atresia. Insist the pathologist reports the exact ratio, because eyeball impressions mislead in tiny samples.
steps.tx: Measure **paucity of interlobular bile ducts** quantitatively on biopsy. Liver biopsy in Alagille syndrome shows a bile duct to portal tract ratio below 0.4 (normal is 0.9 to 1.8), defining ductal paucity (too few small bile ducts). Contrast this with biliary atresia, where ductular proliferation crowds the portal tracts instead. An adequate sample with at least ten portal tracts is mandatory, since tiny biopsies fake both paucity and proliferation convincingly.

steps.say: Genes take weeks, but the bedside already whispers Alagille through five features. Chronic cholestasis with itching, butterfly vertebrae on spine film, posterior embryotoxon on slit lamp, branch pulmonary stenosis murmur, and the triangular facies together make the clinical diagnosis. Three or more features with cholestasis suffice while genes pend. Order the spine film and eye review the same day you suspect it.
steps.tx: Apply the **clinical criteria in Alagille** at the bedside. Clinical criteria include chronic cholestasis, butterfly vertebrae on spine radiographs (split vertebral bodies), posterior embryotoxon on slit-lamp examination (prominent corneal ring), peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis (branch narrowing murmur), and triangular facies (broad forehead, pointed chin). Three major features plus cholestasis support the diagnosis pending genetics. Arrange cardiology, ophthalmology and spinal imaging together, since the syndrome spans all three on day one.

steps.say: Not all inherited cholestasis behaves alike, and one blood value splits the family. When GGT stays normal or low despite deep jaundice, think transporter defects types one and two. When GGT soars, suspect the phospholipid floppase defect of type three. That single enzyme redraws the gene list, the itch severity and the transplant timeline, so check it in every cholestatic infant.
steps.tx: Split **PFIC subtypes by GGT** early. Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC, inherited bile transport failure) types 1 (ATP8B1 gene) and 2 (ABCB11 or BSEP gene) have characteristically normal or low serum GGT, whereas PFIC 3 (ABCB4 or MDR3 gene) has markedly elevated GGT. Low GGT cholestasis with intense pruritus points toward types 1 and 2, while high GGT disease mimics sclerosing patterns. Gene panels confirm the split, but the GGT result available in hours already focuses counselling and surgical planning.

steps.say: For the child scratching through the night despite everything, a new pill blocks bile reabsorption itself. Odevixibat plugs the ileal bile transporter from three months of age, spilling bile acids into the stool and easing the maddening itch. It suits transporter defects best, where the plumbing is intact but the chemistry is wrong. Monitor fat soluble vitamins closely, because looser bile flow can worsen their loss.
steps.tx: Consider **odevixibat ileal bile acid inhibitor** for refractory pruritus. Odevixibat, an oral inhibitor of the ileal bile acid transporter (IBAT, the gut pump reclaiming bile), reduces serum bile acids and pruritus in patients with PFIC aged 3 months and older. Response shows within weeks as scratch scores and bile acids fall, with diarrhoea the commonest side effect. Position it after ursodeoxycholic acid and rifampicin in low GGT disease, and reassess transplant listing once itch and chemistry stabilise.

steps.say: Every cholestatic baby starves of fat soluble vitamins silently, so replace them aggressively from day one. Vitamin A in thousands of units, active vitamin D in fractions of a microgram per kilo, water soluble vitamin E by weight, and vitamin K several times weekly cover the full set. Bleeding, rickets and night blindness are all preventable with this cocktail. Check levels regularly, because cholestasis doses dwarf ordinary supplement doses.
steps.tx: Prescribe **fat-soluble vitamin supplementation** universally in cholestasis. All cholestatic infants require high-dose replacement: Vitamin A (5,000-10,000 IU/day), Vitamin D as calcitriol (0.05-0.2 mcg/kg/day), Vitamin E as TPGS water soluble form (15-25 IU/kg/day), and Vitamin K1 (2.5-5 mg 2-7 times per week). Without bile flow, ordinary multivitamin doses fail completely, risking coagulopathy (bleeding from vitamin K lack), rickets and retinal injury. Monitor levels and clotting at review, adjusting upward whenever cholestasis deepens.
